sets.title: Scrum events: what each one produces
sets.prompt: Match each Scrum event or activity with the output it produces.

pairs.right: A goal for the timebox, selected items, and a plan to deliver them
pairs.lesson: Planning ends with three things: the Sprint Goal, the chosen backlog items, and the developers' plan. If a question asks where the Sprint Backlog is born, it is here.

pairs.right: An adjusted plan for the next day toward the sprint goal
pairs.lesson: This is a planning event for developers, not a status report to the PM. The output is a revised plan; detailed problem-solving happens right after, with only the people needed.

pairs.right: An updated product backlog shaped by stakeholder feedback on the increment
pairs.lesson: Stakeholders see working product and give feedback, and the product owner adjusts the backlog. Trap: it is a working session, not a sign-off ceremony or a slide show.

pairs.right: Actionable improvements to how the team works, carried into the next cycle
pairs.lesson: The retro inspects people, process, tools, and the definition of done. Its output is improvement actions the team owns, so look for it when a question mentions repeating team problems.

pairs.right: Clearer, smaller, estimated items that are ready for upcoming work
pairs.lesson: Refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal Scrum event. The product owner and developers split, clarify, and size items so future planning goes smoothly.

pairs.right: A done, usable increment that meets the agreed quality standard
pairs.lesson: The Sprint is the container for every other event. Whatever else happens, each one should end with at least one usable increment that meets the definition of done.

sets.remember: Plan (goal + backlog) → Daily (adjusted plan) → Review (updated backlog) → Retro (improvements) → Next Sprint

sets.title: Timeboxes and sprint boundaries
sets.prompt: Match each timebox concept with the rule or reason behind it.

pairs.right: A fixed maximum duration that forces focus and value-based choices
pairs.lesson: A timebox caps time and lets scope flex. On the exam, extending a sprint to finish work is the wrong move; the team finishes what it can and re-plans.

pairs.right: A steady cadence that makes velocity useful for forecasting
pairs.lesson: Changing sprint length every cycle breaks the rhythm and makes past velocity meaningless. Teams adjust length only between sprints, after reflecting in a retrospective.

pairs.right: Allowed only by the product owner when the goal becomes obsolete
pairs.lesson: Cancelling is rare and belongs to the product owner alone. A tough sprint or a nervous stakeholder is not a reason; an obsolete goal after a market shift is.

pairs.right: Go back to the product backlog for the product owner to reorder
pairs.lesson: Almost done is not done. Unfinished items are not counted in velocity and are not shown as complete; they return to the backlog and compete again on value.

pairs.right: Clarified or renegotiated with the product owner while protecting the goal
pairs.lesson: The Sprint Backlog is not frozen. Developers adapt it as they learn, but they protect the Sprint Goal and do not quietly add side-door work.

sets.remember: Time is fixed, scope flexes. Same length every sprint. Only the PO cancels. Almost done = not done.

sets.title: Which framework fits this work?
sets.prompt: Match each work situation with the approach and signature practice that fits it best.

pairs.right: Kanban: continuous pull flow with WIP limits, no fixed sprints
pairs.lesson: Variable, interrupt-driven demand suits flow rather than sprints. Her memory line: Kanban hates traffic jams, so stop starting and start finishing.

pairs.left: Many teams building one large solution
pairs.right: SAFe: teams align objectives together in program increment planning
pairs.lesson: When the scenario mentions an agile release train, many teams, or enterprise alignment, think SAFe. The release train engineer facilitates PI planning across teams.

pairs.left: Code quality and frequent releases critical
pairs.right: XP: pair programming, test-first coding, and continuous integration
pairs.lesson: XP is agile with a strict gym trainer. Engineering-practice words like TDD, refactoring, pairing, or CI point straight to Extreme Programming.

pairs.right: Scrum: fixed sprints ending with a review and a retrospective
pairs.lesson: Scrum lives by the calendar. Cadence, defined roles, and inspect-and-adapt events make it a fit for complex products where feedback each cycle matters.

pairs.right: Hybrid: predictive phases for one part, iterations for the other
pairs.lesson: Hybrid is intentional tailoring, not confusion. Stable, regulated components go predictive; uncertain, feedback-driven components go adaptive, with integrated governance.

sets.remember: Scrum gives rhythm • Kanban gives flow • XP gives engineering discipline • SAFe gives scale • Hybrid gives fit

sets.title: Agile metrics: the question each answers
sets.prompt: Match each agile metric with the question it answers.

pairs.right: How many story points does this team finish per sprint?
pairs.lesson: Velocity is a Scrum team's planning and forecasting aid. Trap: it never compares teams or rates individuals, and it is the wrong pick when the scenario says Kanban.

pairs.right: How much planned work still remains before the end date?
pairs.lesson: A burndown slopes down toward zero. It shows remaining work, so it can hide scope growth; that is why some teams prefer a burnup.

pairs.right: How much is complete, and has the total scope grown?
pairs.lesson: A burnup shows completed work rising toward a separate total-scope line. If the top line climbs, scope was added, which a burndown alone can mask.

pairs.right: How long does an item take once work actually starts?
pairs.lesson: Cycle time starts when someone pulls the item into progress. It measures the team's own process speed, a core Kanban flow measure.

pairs.right: How long does a customer wait from request to delivery?
pairs.lesson: Lead time starts the moment the request is made, so it includes queue time before work begins. Customers feel lead time; teams control cycle time.

pairs.right: How many work items get finished in each time period?
pairs.lesson: Throughput counts finished items, not points. It is Kanban's natural partner to velocity: Scrum equals sprint and velocity, Kanban equals flow and throughput.

sets.remember: Velocity = points/sprint • Burndown = remains • Burnup = done • Cycle = once started • Lead = request to delivery • Throughput = items finished

sets.title: Reading agile charts: what the pattern means
sets.prompt: Match each chart pattern with what it most likely tells you.

pairs.right: Work is piling up in that stage, signaling a bottleneck
pairs.lesson: In a cumulative flow diagram, a widening band means items enter a stage faster than they leave. Look there first, then swarm or adjust WIP limits.

pairs.right: Little work is reaching done, so investigate blockers or oversized items
pairs.lesson: A flat burndown can mean impediments, items too big to finish, or work not being marked done. The servant leader response is to investigate, not to blame.

pairs.right: New work is being added to the release faster than planned
pairs.lesson: When the scope line on a burnup climbs, the finish date moves even if the team is productive. Talk with the product owner about trade-offs.

pairs.right: Estimates or team capacity are unstable, so forecasts are unreliable
pairs.lesson: Erratic velocity often comes from changing team membership, inconsistent sizing, or carryover. Discuss causes in the retrospective rather than pressuring for higher numbers.

pairs.left: Lead time grows, cycle time steady
pairs.right: Items are waiting longer in the queue before anyone starts them
pairs.lesson: If the work itself takes the same time but customers wait longer, the delay is before work begins. Fix intake, prioritization, or WIP, not the developers' speed.

sets.remember: Widening band = bottleneck • Flat burndown = stuck • Rising scope line = added work • Lead up, cycle flat = queue

sets.title: Agile estimating: when to use which
sets.prompt: Match each agile estimating practice with the situation where it fits best.

pairs.right: A few refined stories where hidden assumptions need open discussion
pairs.lesson: Everyone reveals a card at once, then the high and low estimators explain. The value is the conversation that surfaces assumptions, not just the number.

pairs.right: A large backlog that must be sized quickly by grouping similar items
pairs.lesson: Teams silently place many items along a scale, then adjust together. Pick it when the scenario stresses speed and volume rather than precision on a few stories.

pairs.right: Early epic or roadmap sizing where only coarse buckets are needed
pairs.lesson: Small, medium, large, extra-large is enough when details are unknown. It supports early roadmap and release conversations before stories are refined.

pairs.right: Team needs a sizing unit that stays stable whoever does the work
pairs.lesson: Points are relative and team-specific. Trap: converting them to hours or comparing them across teams destroys their meaning.

pairs.right: Projecting how many sprints the remaining backlog will likely need
pairs.lesson: Divide remaining points by average velocity to forecast a release range. Use a range, and re-forecast every sprint as real data arrives.

sets.remember: Few stories + talk = Poker • Many items fast = Affinity • Early and rough = T-shirt • Relative size = Points • When will we finish? = Velocity

sets.title: Ready, done, criteria: the question each answers
sets.prompt: Match each agile quality agreement with the question it answers.

pairs.right: Can the team sensibly pull this item into the next sprint?
pairs.lesson: Ready means you are dressed for the wedding. Items are understood, sized, and testable. It is an optional team agreement, not an official Scrum commitment.

pairs.right: Does every increment meet our shared quality and completeness standard?
pairs.lesson: Done means you actually got married. It applies to every item, is owned by the whole Scrum team, and is never relaxed to finish faster.

pairs.right: Does this particular story behave the way the business expects?
pairs.lesson: Criteria are story-specific conditions, usually written with the product owner. A story must satisfy both its own criteria and the shared done standard.

pairs.right: Why is this sprint's work valuable as one coherent whole?
pairs.lesson: The goal gives focus and flexibility: developers can renegotiate individual items while still achieving it. It is created during sprint planning by the Scrum team.

pairs.right: What long-term objective is the whole backlog working toward?
pairs.lesson: This is the commitment for the product backlog, owned by the product owner. Sprint goals are stepping stones toward it.

sets.remember: Ready = can we START? • Done = can we STOP? • Criteria = does THIS story work? • Sprint goal = why this sprint? • Product goal = where the product is heading

sets.title: Servant leadership: what to do now
sets.prompt: Match each team situation with the servant leader's best response.

pairs.right: Help remove the obstacle, escalating only after local attempts fail
pairs.lesson: Removing impediments is the classic servant leader move. Resolve low, escalate high only when needed; calling the sponsor first is a common wrong answer.

pairs.left: Stakeholder hands work straight to developers
pairs.right: Redirect the request to the product owner for backlog ordering
pairs.lesson: No side-door work. The servant leader protects the team's focus and routes new ideas through the backlog front door so value decides priority.

pairs.left: Team asks for daily task assignments
pairs.right: Coach the team to self-manage and choose its own work
pairs.lesson: The PMP favors leadership over micromanagement. Assigning every task undermines ownership; coaching builds a team that plans and commits for itself.

pairs.right: Educate leaders that this measure supports team planning, not appraisal
pairs.lesson: Using team metrics to judge individuals invites inflated estimates and kills collaboration. The servant leader teaches the right use rather than complying silently.

pairs.right: Facilitate so developers plan the next day together toward the goal
pairs.lesson: When the daily event becomes a report to a leader, coach the team back to its purpose: inspecting progress and adapting their own plan.

sets.remember: Serve first: remove impediments • protect focus • coach self-management • teach right metrics • facilitate, don't command

sets.title: Delivery units: MVP, MMF, spike, increment
sets.prompt: Match each agile delivery unit with what it is.

pairs.right: Smallest release built to test a business hypothesis with real users
pairs.lesson: A minimum viable product is about learning: build just enough to validate an assumption. Trap: it is not a low-quality first draft.

pairs.right: Smallest set of functionality that delivers real value when released
pairs.lesson: A minimum marketable feature is about earning value, not just learning. Exam hint: MVP tests whether to build; MMF is the smallest piece worth releasing.

pairs.right: Short, timeboxed research to reduce uncertainty before estimating
pairs.lesson: Use a spike when the team cannot size a story because of a technical or design unknown. Its output is knowledge, often a better estimate.

pairs.right: Usable, done work that adds to everything delivered before it
pairs.lesson: Each one must meet the definition of done and work with all prior increments. Several may be created within one sprint.

pairs.right: Large body of work too big for one sprint, split into smaller pieces
pairs.lesson: Epics sit between roadmap features and stories. They get decomposed during refinement until each piece fits comfortably in a sprint.

pairs.right: Small, testable slice of value written from a customer's viewpoint
pairs.lesson: Classic form: As a role, I want a capability, so that a benefit. Pair it with acceptance criteria so everyone knows when it works.

sets.remember: Vision → Roadmap → Epic → Feature → Story → Acceptance criteria. MVP = learn • MMF = earn • Spike = explore

sets.title: From business need to approved baselines
sets.prompt: Match each early document with what is decided or established at that step.

pairs.right: Leaders judge whether the investment is worth funding at all
pairs.lesson: WHY family. It holds the business need, options, and value. If costs double and leaders ask whether to continue, this is the document they revisit.

pairs.right: Defines how, when, and by whom expected benefits will be measured
pairs.lesson: It travels with the business case and keeps going after the project closes. Benefit owners use it to confirm the value actually arrived.

pairs.right: The sponsor formally authorizes the work and names the PM
pairs.lesson: AUTHORITY family. It turns a justified idea into an authorized project and grants the PM power to use organizational resources.

pairs.right: Subsidiary plans are integrated into one roadmap for managing the work
pairs.lesson: HOW family. It brings together scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, and other plans, plus the baselines, in one approved document.

pairs.right: Integrated scope, schedule, and cost targets approved for measuring performance
pairs.lesson: APPROVED family. Actuals and forecasts are compared against it. It changes only through approved change requests, never because performance slipped.

sets.remember: Need → Business Case (WHY) → Charter (AUTHORITY) → PM Plan (HOW) → Baselines (APPROVED) → Track

sets.title: Requirements to traceability: what feeds what
sets.prompt: Match each scope document with what it feeds into next.

pairs.right: Tells the team whom to involve when eliciting requirements
pairs.lesson: You cannot collect requirements without knowing who holds them. The register lists stakeholders, their interest, and influence, so it feeds requirements elicitation.

pairs.right: Supplies the needs that shape deliverables and traceability rows
pairs.lesson: Each documented requirement should become part of the scope and get a traceability entry. Unrecorded needs become surprise change requests later.

pairs.right: Provides the deliverables that get decomposed into work packages
pairs.lesson: It sets boundaries, exclusions, and acceptance criteria. Decomposing its deliverables is exactly what Create WBS does.

pairs.right: Joins its dictionary and the statement to form the approved scope baseline
pairs.lesson: Scope baseline equals scope statement plus WBS plus WBS dictionary. Once approved, its content changes only through change control.

pairs.right: Links each requirement to tests used before customer acceptance
pairs.lesson: TRACE family. It carries a requirement from origin to deliverable to test to status, so it supports Validate Scope and proves nothing was missed.

sets.remember: WHO (stakeholders) → WHAT (requirements) → BOUNDARIES (scope statement) → STRUCTURE (WBS) → TRACE (RTM)

sets.title: Trigger words: which document to open
sets.prompt: Match each trigger word with the document it should make you think of.

pairs.right: Risk register entry with probability, impact, owner, and response
pairs.lesson: Words like may, might, possible, or uncertain point to a risk. Log and analyze it before acting; it is not yet a problem to resolve.

pairs.right: Issue log entry with owner, action, and target resolution date
pairs.lesson: Words like already, currently, or discovered mean the event is real. Manage it as an issue now, and update related risk information too.

pairs.right: Matrix linking each requirement to its origin, deliverable, and test
pairs.lesson: When the scenario asks which test proves a requirement was met, or where a requirement came from, open the RTM.

pairs.right: Dictionary entry describing a work package's criteria, owner, and milestones
pairs.lesson: The WBS gives structure; its dictionary gives the detail behind each box. Structure, detail, trace is her three-word chant.

pairs.right: Log showing which requests were approved, rejected, or deferred
pairs.lesson: The change log records outcomes; the change management plan describes the process. Trap: logging a request does not approve it.

pairs.right: Signed agreement stating legal obligations, price, and remedies
pairs.lesson: Any question about what a vendor must do or be paid goes to the contract. The PM manages seller performance but cannot rewrite its terms alone.

sets.remember: MAY HAPPEN → Risk Register • HAPPENED → Issue Log • TRACE → RTM • DETAIL → WBS Dictionary • CHANGE STATUS → Change Log • SELLER → Contract

sets.title: How each document type may change
sets.prompt: Match each type of project document with how it is allowed to change.

pairs.right: Revised through governance when the way we manage must change
pairs.lesson: Plans are the HOW family and sit in the yellow zone: the PM can propose updates, but changes follow the plan's own governance.

pairs.right: Moves only after an authorized change request is approved
pairs.lesson: Baselines are red zone. Poor CPI is never a reason to rebaseline; analyze, forecast, and use change control only for real authorized changes.

pairs.right: Updated freely by the PM and owners as reality shifts
pairs.lesson: Living records are green zone. Adding risks, updating ratings, and recording responses is normal ongoing work, no approval needed.

pairs.right: Recalculated from actual performance whenever new data arrives
pairs.lesson: Forecasts move with reality; baselines move with approval. A worse EAC is information to act on, not a change to the approved budget.

pairs.right: Amended only through its change clause with procurement authority
pairs.lesson: Contracts are legal documents. Even when the PM agrees with a seller, contract changes need the authorized contract change process and possibly project change control.

pairs.right: Reissued each cycle to communicate analyzed status to stakeholders
pairs.lesson: Reports are the COMMUNICATE family. Data is raw, information is analyzed, reports are packaged and sent to the people who need them.

sets.remember: Living documents evolve. Plans follow governance. Baselines and contracts change only through authorized approval.

sets.title: Which document to check first
sets.prompt: Match each scenario with the document the PM should check first.

pairs.right: Change management plan, which sets authority levels and thresholds
pairs.lesson: Before routing a request, check the defined process. Not every change goes to a CCB; the plan says who decides what and at which threshold.

pairs.right: Communications management plan, which lists who gets what and when
pairs.lesson: Communication preferences live in the plan. Check it, then update it through normal governance if the stakeholder's need is legitimate.

pairs.right: Business case, which justifies whether the investment still makes sense
pairs.lesson: Worth-it questions are WHY questions. The sponsor revisits the business case to decide whether to continue, change, or stop.

pairs.right: Scope baseline, holding the approved statement, WBS, and dictionary
pairs.lesson: Check the approved scope before saying yes or no. If it is outside, it becomes a change request, not quiet extra work.

pairs.right: Team charter, holding the ground rules the team agreed together
pairs.lesson: Go back to the team's own agreements first and talk privately with the person. Escalating to a manager is not the first step.

pairs.right: Contract, which states agreed price, terms, and change clauses
pairs.lesson: Review the agreement before negotiating. Contract first, document everything, negotiate before escalating.

sets.remember: FIRST = check the right document: Process? Plan. Worth it? Business case. In scope? Baseline. Team norms? Team charter. Seller? Contract.

sets.title: Procurement asks and seller answers
sets.prompt: Match each procurement item with what the seller sends back or what happens with it.

pairs.right: Seller returns an information response about its capabilities; no award yet
pairs.lesson: A request for information explores the market early. Nobody wins a contract from an RFI; it helps the buyer shape later solicitation.

pairs.right: Seller returns a price quotation for clearly specified items
pairs.lesson: Use it when specs are clear and price is the main comparison. Trap: an RFQ is wrong for complex work where the approach matters.

pairs.right: Seller returns a proposal describing its solution approach, value, and price
pairs.lesson: Use it when the problem is complex and you want vendors to propose how. Info, solution, price: RFI, RFP, RFQ.

pairs.right: Seller returns a formal sealed offer against fixed, comparable specifications
pairs.lesson: An invitation for bid suits well-defined work where offers can be compared directly. The seller's response is called a bid.

pairs.right: Buyer's weighted yardstick for scoring every seller response fairly
pairs.lesson: Written by the buyer before responses arrive. Trap: lowest price is not automatically best, and a sponsor's favorite vendor still gets scored on the criteria.

pairs.right: Buyer answers all prospective sellers' questions together and equally
pairs.lesson: It keeps the process fair so no seller gets inside information. Clarifications are shared with every bidder.

sets.remember: Buyer asks. Seller responds. Both sign. INFO → RFI • PRICE → RFQ • SOLUTION → RFP • FORMAL BID → IFB

sets.title: Procurement documents: what each holds
sets.prompt: Match each procurement document with what it holds.

pairs.right: How this project will buy goods and services, from start to finish
pairs.lesson: A HOW-family subsidiary plan written by the PM with procurement input. When a question asks how purchasing is run or who may sign, look here first.

pairs.right: The request package sent out so vendors can prepare responses
pairs.lesson: RFI, RFQ, RFP and IFB are all bid documents, issued by the buyer. Trap: they invite offers; nothing is binding yet and no seller is chosen.

pairs.right: A vendor's written answer describing its approach, price, and qualifications
pairs.lesson: Written by each seller, never by the buyer, and scored against source selection criteria. Trap: a proposal is only an offer until both sides sign.

pairs.right: Legally binding record of obligations, price, terms, and remedies
pairs.lesson: Also called the contract: the SELLER family. Signed by people with authority on both sides. Changes follow its change clause; the PM cannot rewrite terms alone.

pairs.right: Buyer's documented review of how well a vendor actually delivered
pairs.lesson: Prepared by the buyer during Control Procurements. It records quality, timeliness and cooperation, and shapes whether that vendor stays on qualified seller lists.

pairs.right: Complete indexed set of contract records archived at closure
pairs.lesson: Contracts, amendments, invoices, claims and correspondence kept together. It is archived into organizational process assets and supports audits or later disputes.

sets.remember: Plan (how we buy) → Bid documents (buyer asks) → Proposal (seller answers) → Agreement (both sign) → Performance review → File (archive)

sets.title: Inside the WBS: decomposition levels
sets.prompt: Match each WBS element or rule with what it means.

pairs.right: Unique, verifiable product or result shown at an upper level
pairs.lesson: WBS elements are nouns, not verbs. Deliverables are decomposed until the pieces are small enough to estimate and manage.

pairs.right: Management point where scope, budget, and actual cost are compared
pairs.lesson: It sits above work packages and is where earned value is often measured. Each one belongs to a single responsible manager.

pairs.right: Lowest level, where cost and duration are estimated and managed
pairs.lesson: It is the bottom of the WBS. Exam trap: work packages are not activities; they are decomposed into activities during schedule planning.

pairs.right: Placeholder with known scope but no detailed activities yet
pairs.lesson: This is rolling wave planning inside predictive work. It sits under a control account and gets detailed as information arrives.

pairs.right: Scheduled action decomposed from the lowest element, outside the structure
pairs.lesson: Activities live in the activity list and schedule, not in the WBS. Verb phrases like pour the slab signal an activity.

pairs.right: Children together capture all the work and only that work
pairs.lesson: Nothing missing, nothing extra. If work is not in the WBS, it is not in the project scope; extra work such as gold plating sits outside the approved scope.

sets.remember: Scope statement → Deliverable → Control account → Work package → Activity (schedule). Structure, detail, trace.

sets.title: Closing documents and what they capture
sets.prompt: Match each closing document with what it captures or where it goes.

pairs.right: Formal sign-off proving the customer agreed the criteria were met
pairs.lesson: Verified is internal; accepted is formal. These records come from Validate Scope and are required before closure can be completed.

pairs.right: Summary of scope, schedule, cost, quality, and benefit results versus objectives
pairs.lesson: It tells the story of the whole project for the sponsor and organization, including whether the business need was met.

pairs.right: Living record updated throughout, then moved to organizational assets
pairs.lesson: Do not wait until the end. Capture lessons after milestones, apply them immediately, and archive the register at closing.

pairs.right: Organizational knowledge base that future teams search during planning
pairs.lesson: It is an organizational process asset, not a project document. The register feeds it; new projects draw from it.

pairs.right: Move the product, support duties, and knowledge to the receiving owners
pairs.lesson: Transfer is a real step: training, support agreements, and documentation so operations can sustain the product and benefits.

pairs.right: Confirm seller work accepted, claims settled, and agreement formally ended
pairs.lesson: Each contract is closed per its terms. Open claims must be settled, ideally by negotiation, before the procurement is formally closed.

sets.remember: Complete → Accept → Transfer → Learn → Close. Register is living; repository is forever.

sets.title: Change requests: who does each step
sets.prompt: Match each step of the change request journey with who does it and how.

pairs.right: Any stakeholder may submit one in writing through the process
pairs.lesson: Anyone can raise a change, including team members and customers. Verbal requests should be documented so they can be analyzed properly.

pairs.right: PM and team assess effects on scope, time, cost, and risk
pairs.lesson: The CCB is a judge, not an investigator. The PM brings a fully analyzed request with options; analyze with the team before going to the board.

pairs.right: CCB or designated authority per the defined thresholds
pairs.lesson: The change management plan names who decides. Small changes may sit within PM authority; baseline changes usually go to the board.

pairs.right: Approved, rejected, or deferred status is written in the log
pairs.lesson: Every decision gets recorded, including rejections. The log tracks status; it does not grant approval by itself.

pairs.right: PM revises affected documents only after approval is granted
pairs.lesson: Update first, then implement and communicate. Changing the baseline before approval is a classic wrong answer.

pairs.right: Follows the same formal process; seniority grants no bypass
pairs.lesson: Even the sponsor submits a change request. The PM analyzes impact and routes it properly rather than simply complying.

sets.remember: Request → Analyze → Decide → Record → Update plans → Communicate → Implement → Monitor. Anyone raises • PM analyzes • CCB decides • Log records

sets.title: Plans, baselines, reserves: who controls them
sets.prompt: Match each planning item with who controls changes to it or its use.

pairs.right: PM develops it with the team; sponsor and key stakeholders approve
pairs.lesson: The PM integrates all subsidiary plans, but approval comes from the people with authority. After approval, changes follow integrated change control.

pairs.right: Changes only after the change board approves a formal request
pairs.lesson: The PM cannot rebaseline alone, even if the PM created it. Protected does not mean impossible; it means authorized.

pairs.right: PM may apply it to identified risks as the plan allows
pairs.lesson: It covers known-unknowns and is inside the cost baseline. Using it for a planned risk response does not need a baseline change.

pairs.right: Released by management for unforeseen work, then the baseline is updated
pairs.lesson: It covers unknown-unknowns and sits outside the cost baseline. Using it requires management approval and a change to the baseline.

pairs.right: PM updates it from actual performance without needing approval
pairs.lesson: Forecasts are the PM's to maintain. Sharing a worse forecast honestly is required; changing the budget to match it is not allowed.

sets.remember: PM develops • Stakeholders approve • CCB guards baselines • PM uses contingency • Management releases reserve • PM forecasts

sets.title: RACI roles in practice
sets.prompt: Match each RACI role or rule with what it means for a task.

pairs.right: Does the work to complete the task; there may be several
pairs.lesson: R is the doer. Many people can share it. Trap: the person doing the work is not automatically the one who answers for the result.

pairs.right: The single person who answers for the result and signs off
pairs.lesson: Only one A per task, so ownership is never ambiguous. The A may delegate the work but not the ownership.

pairs.right: Gives input before or during the work in two-way conversation
pairs.lesson: These are subject experts or affected parties whose opinion is sought. Too many C's slow everything down.

pairs.right: Kept up to date on progress or decisions in one-way updates
pairs.lesson: They need to know, not to contribute. Use this to plan push communications without inviting them to every meeting.

pairs.right: Ownership is unclear, so fix the matrix to one name
pairs.lesson: Two A's on one row is a design flaw that causes finger-pointing. Resolve it with the stakeholders and update the matrix.

sets.remember: R = does it • A = owns it (only one!) • C = asked before • I = told after

sets.title: Governance bodies and PMO types
sets.prompt: Match each governance body or PMO type with its role and level of control.

pairs.right: Offers templates, training, and lessons; low control over projects
pairs.lesson: Supportive equals Help. It acts as a resource library and coach, and project managers are free to choose whether to use its materials.

pairs.right: Requires compliance with methods, templates, and audits; moderate control
pairs.lesson: Controlling equals Rules. It checks that projects follow standards and may review or audit them, but it does not run them.

pairs.right: Directly manages projects and assigns project managers; high control
pairs.lesson: Directive equals Runs. Project managers report to it, so it holds the most control of the three types.

pairs.right: Senior group setting direction and deciding matters beyond PM thresholds
pairs.lesson: Escalate here when budget, strategy, or cross-project decisions exceed the PM's authority, such as overruns beyond contingency.

pairs.right: Formally reviews requests and approves, rejects, or defers them
pairs.lesson: The board decides on changes as defined in the change management plan. It does not investigate; the PM brings an analyzed request.

sets.remember: Supportive = Help • Controlling = Rules • Directive = Runs • Steering committee = direction • CCB = change decisions

sets.title: Who to go to: the right door
sets.prompt: Match each situation with who the PM should go to and how.

pairs.right: Negotiate with that manager first; senior management if still unresolved
pairs.lesson: In a matrix, the functional manager owns the person. Discuss impact and priorities directly before taking it higher.

pairs.right: Sponsor or the governance path defined for that decision
pairs.lesson: Do not make an unauthorized decision, and do not freeze. Check the escalation path and bring the right authority in with analysis.

pairs.right: Steering committee or management that controls the reserve
pairs.lesson: Once contingency is spent, the PM lacks authority to fund more. Present the analysis and options to whoever holds management reserve.

pairs.right: Scrum master or PM works to remove it, escalating only if needed
pairs.lesson: Resolve low first. If the team can fix it, they do; if facilitation helps, the servant leader steps in; outside authority comes last.

pairs.right: Talk privately first, referring to the team's agreed norms
pairs.lesson: Never go to the functional manager first for a team behavior issue. Private conversation, then coaching, then formal escalation if unresolved.

pairs.right: Negotiate per the agreement, then its dispute clause and procurement authority
pairs.lesson: Contract first. Notify in writing, negotiate in good faith, then use ADR or the contract's escalation steps; litigation is last.

sets.remember: Problem → Assess → Check owner → Act at lowest level → Escalate only when needed, to the right door

sets.title: Who verifies, who accepts
sets.prompt: Match each role with its part in getting a deliverable verified or accepted.

pairs.right: Inspects and tests outputs against specifications; an internal check only
pairs.lesson: Control Quality produces verified deliverables. Passing internal tests does not mean the customer has accepted anything.

pairs.right: Formally signs off that acceptance criteria were met
pairs.lesson: Validate Scope is where formal acceptance happens, with the authorized party. Their sign-off turns a verified deliverable into an accepted one.

pairs.right: Decides whether sprint work meets the stated story criteria
pairs.lesson: On agile work, the product owner represents the customer's view of value and judges whether items fulfil their criteria.

pairs.right: Facilitates and records acceptance but cannot sign for the customer
pairs.lesson: The PM organizes the review and keeps the records. Claiming acceptance on the customer's behalf is a trap answer.

pairs.right: Build quality in so each sprint item meets the team's shared standard
pairs.lesson: Developers are accountable for building quality in. Items that miss the definition of done are not shown as complete.

pairs.right: Confirms seller deliverables are accepted before closing the agreement
pairs.lesson: For procured work, formal acceptance of seller deliverables follows the contract and is required before procurement closure.

sets.remember: Create → Control Quality (verified) → Validate Scope (accepted) → Transition. Verified is internal; accepted is formal.

sets.title: Mid-sprint: who may change what
sets.prompt: Match each agile item with who may change it and when.

pairs.right: Product owner may reorder anytime; others influence but cannot dictate
pairs.lesson: Stakeholders, including executives, bring requests to the product owner. Nobody else reorders the list directly.

pairs.right: Developers adapt it daily as they learn, protecting the goal
pairs.lesson: This belongs to the developers. The product owner does not assign tasks inside it, and the Scrum Master does not own it either.

pairs.right: Fixed for the sprint; if obsolete, the product owner cancels
pairs.lesson: The goal is the sprint's anchor. Scope can be renegotiated around it, but swapping the goal mid-sprint means cancelling and re-planning.

pairs.right: Scrum team may strengthen it; never relaxed to finish faster
pairs.lesson: Owned by the whole Scrum team, or set by the organization as a minimum. Lowering quality to hit a date is the classic trap.

pairs.right: Scrum team adjusts it between sprints, never during one
pairs.lesson: Changing cadence is a retrospective decision. Extending the current sprint to finish work breaks the timebox.

sets.remember: PO = WHAT/WHY (backlog order) • Developers = HOW (sprint plan) • Scrum team = standards (DoD, cadence)

sets.title: Who authors each document
sets.prompt: Match each document with who creates it.

pairs.right: Prepared on the business side before the project exists
pairs.lesson: It is a pre-project business document. The PM may help update it later, but it is owned outside the project by the sponsor or business.

pairs.right: Issued by the sponsor or initiator from outside the team
pairs.lesson: The PM may help draft it, but issuing authority sits with someone who can fund and authorize the work.

pairs.right: Developed by the PM with the team, then approved by stakeholders
pairs.lesson: The PM integrates the plan and does not write it alone. Involving the team builds better estimates and commitment.

pairs.right: Created by the team members together, facilitated rather than imposed
pairs.lesson: Values, norms, decision rules, and conflict process belong to the team. Imposed rules get ignored; agreed rules get followed.

pairs.right: Written by the buyer's team from the approved scope
pairs.lesson: The buyer describes the work it wants. Sellers never write the statement they are bidding against.

pairs.right: Written by each vendor in response to the buyer's request
pairs.lesson: Buyer asks, seller responds. The proposal answers an RFP with the seller's solution, approach, and price.

sets.remember: Business decides WHY • Sponsor issues AUTHORITY • PM + team plan HOW • Team writes its norms • Buyer asks, seller answers

sets.title: Risk roles: who does what
sets.prompt: Match each role with its responsibility for project risk.

pairs.right: Leads the overall process and keeps the register current
pairs.lesson: The PM manages the risk process and the register, but does not personally own every individual risk.

pairs.right: Watches triggers and carries out the agreed response for an assigned risk
pairs.lesson: Every important risk needs a named owner. If nobody owns the risk, everybody assumes somebody else is watching it.

pairs.right: Performs a specific task assigned within an agreed response
pairs.lesson: Larger responses can have several actions. The owner of the risk coordinates them; action owners do the individual pieces.

pairs.right: Identify new uncertainties continuously, not only in workshops
pairs.lesson: Risk identification is iterative and everyone's job. Raise a possible threat as soon as it is noticed, then log and analyze it.

pairs.right: Sets tolerance levels and receives risks beyond project authority
pairs.lesson: When a risk is outside the project's scope or authority, escalate it to the sponsor or program, who then owns the decision.

sets.remember: PM runs the process • Owner watches and responds • Action owner does the task • Team identifies • Sponsor takes escalations

sets.title: Change control: the detailed path
sets.prompt: Match each step of the detailed change control path with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Pin down exactly what is being asked, by whom, and why
pairs.lesson: Before any analysis, make sure you understand the request itself. A customer asking for something is a trigger to clarify and analyze, never a reason to implement on the spot.

pairs.right: Evaluate effects on scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality and value
pairs.lesson: Her ripple flow applies here: Scope → Schedule → Cost → Resources → Risk → Value. The PM analyzes and brings options to the decision makers; the PM does not decide alone.

pairs.right: Board or named authority approves, rejects, or defers the request
pairs.lesson: Who decides is written in the change management plan, often a change control board. Rejected requests still get recorded in the change log so the history is traceable.

pairs.right: Bring the approved documents and targets in line with the authorized change
pairs.lesson: Only an approved change may touch a baseline. Trap: updating the baseline first, or rebaselining just to hide a poor CPI. Baselines are the APPROVED family.

pairs.right: Tell the team and affected stakeholders what changed and when
pairs.lesson: Follow the communications management plan so everyone works from the new version. Skipping this step is how teams keep building to an outdated requirement.

pairs.right: Team performs the authorized work and results are tracked against the new plan
pairs.lesson: Implementation happens only after authorization. In an agile setting the same idea shows up as a reprioritized backlog item rather than a board decision.

sets.remember: Change identified → Clarify → Impact analysis → Formal approval path → Decision → Update plans/baselines → Communicate → Implement → Monitor (hook: Request → Analyze → Authorize → Update → Implement → Watch)

sets.title: Risk to issue: the life of a risk
sets.prompt: Match each step of the risk flow with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Record an uncertain future event with its cause, effect, and owner
pairs.lesson: Identified risks go into the risk register with an owner. Trap: something already happening is not a risk; it belongs in the issue log right away.

pairs.right: Rate probability and impact to decide which ones deserve attention
pairs.lesson: Qualitative analysis (probability and impact matrix) ranks them; quantitative analysis such as Monte Carlo or EMV puts numbers on the important few. Analysis comes before choosing a response.

pairs.right: Choose avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept or escalate and name an owner
pairs.lesson: Opportunities use exploit, enhance, share, accept or escalate. Each response has an owner, may draw on contingency reserve, and can create secondary risks to watch.

pairs.right: Watch warning signs and check that planned actions still work
pairs.lesson: Monitor Risks runs all project long: track triggers, review residual and secondary risks, and identify new risks in reviews and retrospectives.

pairs.right: The event has happened, so it is now handled as an issue
pairs.lesson: Her rule: once it happens, it becomes an issue. Carry out the planned response or a workaround. Trap: jumping to a contract claim or rebaselining first.

pairs.right: Close or revise the risk entry and the issue log, then capture lessons
pairs.lesson: Close or update the risk entry, open or update the issue entry, and capture the lesson. These are TRACK documents the PM keeps current without board approval.

sets.remember: Identify → Analyze → Plan response → Monitor triggers → Occurs = Issue → Update both records (Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue)

sets.title: Stakeholder and conflict flow, step by step
sets.prompt: Match each step of the stakeholder and conflict flow with what the project manager does at that step.

pairs.right: Listen first and learn each party's concerns, facts, and interests
pairs.lesson: Her golden rule: collaborate before escalating, and that starts with talking to the person. Use active listening, paraphrase, ask clarifying questions and acknowledge emotions before proposing any fix.

pairs.right: Judge the effect on scope, schedule, relationships and project goals
pairs.lesson: Check the stakeholder register, engagement matrix and team charter. Is this a real project impact? Remember personality is the least common source of conflict.

pairs.right: Bring the people involved together to work out a shared solution
pairs.lesson: Collaborate/problem solve is PMI's default win-win mode. The PM facilitates while the people who own the problem help solve it, which builds commitment.

pairs.right: Carry out the agreed action and update the relevant documents
pairs.lesson: Agreed actions need an owner and a date. Update the issue log, stakeholder engagement plan or team charter so the agreement actually sticks.

pairs.right: Follow up to confirm the agreement holds and engagement improves
pairs.lesson: Monitor Stakeholder Engagement compares current with desired engagement. One conversation is not a resolution; check back and adjust your approach.

pairs.right: Raise to sponsor or functional manager only when beyond PM authority
pairs.lesson: Escalation is the last step, not the first. Trap answers send a team conflict straight to the sponsor or HR before the PM has tried to resolve it.

sets.remember: Understand → Assess → Collaborate → Act → Monitor → Escalate

sets.title: Closing a project: the full checklist
sets.prompt: Match each step of the detailed closing flow with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Check that the exit conditions in the charter and plan are met
pairs.lesson: Exit criteria come from the charter and project management plan. Even a project terminated early is closed formally, with the reason documented.

pairs.right: Customer or sponsor signs off that deliverables meet agreed criteria
pairs.lesson: Accepted deliverables come from Validate Scope. Trap: passing internal testing means verified, not accepted. Acceptance always comes from the customer or sponsor.

pairs.right: Hand the product to operations or the customer with support knowledge
pairs.lesson: This is the Transfer step in her short flow. Plan training, documentation and support early; benefits usually appear after handover, owned by operations.

pairs.right: Verify seller work, settle payments and claims, and end contracts
pairs.lesson: Contracts are closed before the project is. Settle open claims, ideally by negotiation, and use a procurement audit to capture what worked with each seller.

pairs.right: Summarize performance on scope, schedule, cost, quality and benefits
pairs.lesson: The final report tells the project's story to the sponsor. Lessons learned are finalized and archived to organizational process assets at the same time.

pairs.right: Free people, equipment and facilities once their work is truly done
pairs.lesson: Release after acceptance and knowledge capture, not before, because you need people for lessons learned. Recognizing the team fits Tuckman's Adjourning stage.

sets.remember: Confirm criteria → Accept → Transition → Close contracts → Final report → Lessons/archive → Release resources → Formal closure (hook: Confirm → Accept → Transfer → Close → Archive)

sets.title: Procurement flow from need to closure
sets.prompt: Match each step of the procurement flow with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Decide whether to do the work internally or buy it from outside
pairs.lesson: Part of Plan Procurement Management. Weigh cost, capability, risk and confidentiality. The make-or-buy decision drives every later step in the procurement flow.

pairs.right: Describe the purchased work in enough detail for sellers to price it
pairs.lesson: The buyer writes it, derived from the scope baseline. A vague statement of work leads to poor bids and later claims. It goes out with the RFQ, RFP or IFB.

pairs.right: Give every prospective seller the same information and answers together
pairs.lesson: The point is fairness and shared understanding before bids are due. Trap: answering one seller privately. Questions and answers are shared with all bidders.

pairs.right: Score responses against source selection criteria to choose a seller
pairs.lesson: Criteria are set before responses arrive. Her trap: lowest price is not always best for complex work. RFQ suits a clear, price-only comparison.

pairs.right: Manage the seller relationship, performance, payments and contract changes
pairs.lesson: The contract governs. Contract changes go through the contract change control system, and only the authorized buyer can change the contract. Negotiate before escalating.

pairs.right: Confirm accepted deliverables, resolve claims, and formally complete the agreement
pairs.lesson: Settle claims (negotiation first), make final payments, archive records and run a procurement audit. In PMBOK 6 this closure sits inside Control Procurements.

sets.remember: Plan → Make-or-buy → SOW → Solicit → Bidder conference → Evaluate → Select → Contract → Control → Close (Define clearly • Select fairly • Monitor actively • Change formally • Close cleanly)

sets.title: Compliance flow: the question at each step
sets.prompt: Match each step of the compliance flow with the question the project manager asks at that step.

pairs.right: Does this new law or standard actually cover our project?
pairs.lesson: Not every regulation in the news touches your project, so check first. Once it does apply, her rule kicks in: mandatory beats optional.

pairs.right: What will it change in our scope, schedule, cost and risk?
pairs.lesson: Impact assessment shows the size of the work, not whether to do it. Compliance is never traded away because it is expensive or late.

pairs.right: What do legal, compliance or specialist advisors say it requires?
pairs.lesson: The PM is not the lawyer. Bring in legal, the compliance office or SMEs to interpret the requirement before deciding the response.

pairs.right: Which specific work, controls or requirements must we now add?
pairs.lesson: Turn the rule into concrete project work: new requirements, controls, tests or documents. In agile, these items rise to the top of the backlog or join the definition of done.

pairs.right: Has the new work gone through change control into our approved documents?
pairs.lesson: Even mandatory work goes through the change process so baselines and the RTM stay accurate. Mandatory means no debate on whether, not skipping governance.

pairs.right: Can we prove we meet it with evidence, testing or an audit?
pairs.lesson: Compliance must be demonstrable. Keep evidence, run audits or checks, and keep monitoring because regulations change over time.

sets.remember: Requirement emerges → Confirm applicability → Assess impact → Consult experts → Determine changes → Update plans/backlog → Implement → Measure compliance (hook: Law → Applies? → Impact → Expert → Change → Comply)

sets.title: Quality flow: plan, build, check, accept
sets.prompt: Match each step of the quality flow with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Decide which standards apply and how they will be met and checked
pairs.lesson: Produces the quality management plan and metrics. Remember cost of quality: prevention is cheaper than inspection, and inspection is cheaper than defects reaching the customer.

pairs.right: Set measurable targets such as defect rate or response time
pairs.lesson: A metric states exactly what is measured and the tolerance. Without it, Control Quality has nothing objective to check against.

pairs.right: Audit processes and improve how work is done to prevent defects
pairs.lesson: This is quality assurance: process-focused, using audits and process improvement. Trap: it does not inspect the deliverable itself, that is Control Quality.

pairs.right: Inspect and test the outputs to produce verified deliverables
pairs.lesson: Internal check of correctness, usually by the team or QC. Its output, verified deliverables, is the input to Validate Scope.

pairs.right: Repair nonconforming items, find the root cause, and recheck them
pairs.lesson: Defect repair is a type of change request. Use root cause analysis such as fishbone or five whys so the defect does not come back.

pairs.right: Customer or sponsor formally signs off on the verified work
pairs.lesson: External acceptance. Order matters: Control Quality first (correct), then Validate Scope (accepted). Accepted deliverables later feed Close Project.

sets.remember: Plan Quality → Define metrics → Manage Quality → Control Quality → Correct defects → Verify → Validate Scope (hook: Plan quality → Build quality → Check quality → Accept quality)

sets.title: Issue escalation path
sets.prompt: Match each step of the issue path with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Capture the problem, date raised and its impact as soon as it appears
pairs.lesson: An issue is a problem happening now, so it goes in the issue log, not the risk register. The PM keeps this TRACK document current without board approval.

pairs.right: Find why it happened and what it affects before fixing it
pairs.lesson: Fixing symptoms lets the problem return. Use data, five whys or a fishbone, and check knock-on effects on scope, schedule and cost.

pairs.right: Give one named person accountability and a target date
pairs.lesson: Every issue entry has a single owner and due date. Unowned issues are the ones that drift until they become crises.

pairs.right: Team or PM applies a fix using their own decision rights
pairs.lesson: Most issues are solved inside the team. In agile, the team owns its own blockers first and the scrum master removes what the team cannot.

pairs.right: Raise to sponsor or governance when impact exceeds agreed thresholds
pairs.lesson: Escalate only when the fix is outside your authority or the impact breaks agreed tolerances. Trap: escalating before analyzing or trying to resolve.

pairs.right: Confirm the fix worked, then record the outcome and lessons
pairs.lesson: Monitor before closing: the fix must actually work. Then update the issue log and lessons learned register so others benefit.

sets.remember: Issue occurs → Log → Analyze → Assign owner → Resolve → Escalate only if beyond authority → Monitor → Close (hook: Log → Understand → Own → Fix → Watch → Close)

sets.title: Benefits flow: from need to value
sets.prompt: Match each step of the benefits flow with what happens at that step.

pairs.right: Business case states the measurable gains that justify the investment
pairs.lesson: The business case is the WHY family. It is written before the charter and revisited at gates to check the investment is still worth it.

pairs.right: A formal document setting when and how the gains will be realized and sustained
pairs.lesson: Usually developed by the sponsor with the PM's help. It names targets, timing, metrics and owners, and often covers time after project closure.

pairs.right: Assign a benefit owner and pick the KPI that proves each gain
pairs.lesson: A benefit owner, often in the business or operations, is accountable for realizing it. Without a KPI, nobody can prove the benefit arrived.

pairs.right: Project produces the deliverables, such as a new app or process
pairs.lesson: Outputs are what you build. Trap: finishing deliverables on time does not by itself mean the project created value.

pairs.right: Users adopt the product and their capability or behavior changes
pairs.lesson: Outcomes need adoption, so organizational change work such as training and reinforcement matters here. No adoption, no outcome.

pairs.right: Track KPIs, often after closure, to confirm the promised gains appeared
pairs.lesson: Benefits often show up after handover, so ownership transitions to operations. Compare actual results with the business case targets.

sets.remember: Define benefits → Benefits plan → Measures/owners → Outputs → Outcomes → Measure benefits → Transition ownership (Output → Outcome → Benefit → Value)

sets.title: Tuckman in real life: read the moment
sets.prompt: Match each team moment with the stage it signals and the project manager's best move.

pairs.right: Forming: give direction, clarify goals and roles, start the team charter
pairs.lesson: Polite and uncertain is the signal. The PM is more directive here. Her first action for a new team: build or review the team charter together.

pairs.right: Storming: coach, mediate and enforce ground rules rather than avoiding it
pairs.lesson: Storming is necessary and normal; performance dips before it recovers. Trap answers replace a member or escalate. Coach through it and use collaborate/problem solve.

pairs.left: Team drafts its own working agreements
pairs.right: Norming: reinforce the agreements and encourage shared ownership
pairs.lesson: Working agreements emerging is the classic Norming sign. The PM steps back a little, supports, and reinforces collaboration and trust.

pairs.left: Team self-organizes and hits its goals
pairs.right: Performing: delegate, empower, and focus on clearing impediments
pairs.lesson: A high-performing team needs less direction, not more. Micromanaging now is a wrong answer; servant leadership and impediment removal fit best.

pairs.right: Adjourning: recognize contributions, capture lessons, release people
pairs.lesson: Celebrate and recognize, finalize lessons learned, and release resources properly. Adjourning was added later to Tuckman's original four stages.

pairs.right: Expect a slide back to Storming: onboard deliberately, revisit the charter
pairs.lesson: Teams can regress when membership changes. Re-run onboarding, revisit the team charter together, and expect a short performance dip.

sets.remember: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning (direct → coach → support → delegate → celebrate; new members = possible reset)

sets.title: Motivation theories: putting them to work
sets.prompt: Match each motivation theory with how a project manager would apply it.

pairs.right: Find the lowest unmet need, such as belonging for an isolated remote member
pairs.lesson: Lower needs come first: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualization. Example: an isolated remote member has a social gap, so praise for esteem alone will not fix it.

pairs.right: Fix pay and conditions to stop complaints, then add growth to truly motivate
pairs.lesson: Hygiene factors like salary and conditions only prevent dissatisfaction. Motivators like recognition, responsibility and growth create satisfaction. A raise alone rarely motivates for long.

pairs.right: Give achievers stretch goals, affiliators team roles, power-seekers leadership chances
pairs.lesson: People have a dominant need for achievement, affiliation or power. Match the assignment to the person's dominant need instead of treating everyone the same.

pairs.right: Assume people want to do good work and give autonomy over tight control
pairs.lesson: Theory X assumes people dislike work and need control; Theory Y assumes they are self-motivated. PMI and agile teams lean strongly toward Y.

pairs.right: Make sure effort can lead to results and the reward is actually valued
pairs.lesson: Effort → Performance → Reward. If people think the target is impossible or do not value the reward, motivation collapses. Check all three links.

pairs.right: Build long-term commitment through group decisions and care for wellbeing
pairs.lesson: Rooted in Japanese management: long-term employment, collective decision-making and concern for the whole person. Think loyalty and shared ownership over time.

sets.remember: Maslow = lowest need first • Herzberg = hygiene vs motivators • McClelland = achieve/affiliate/power • X/Y = control vs trust • Vroom = effort → performance → valued reward • Z = long-term + collective

sets.title: Conflict modes: when each one fits
sets.prompt: Match each conflict resolution mode with the situation where it is the right choice.

pairs.right: Time allows and both sides need a lasting win-win answer
pairs.lesson: PMI's default and usually the best exam answer: confront the problem, address root cause, and build a solution both sides fully own.

pairs.right: Deadline is tight and equal-power parties accept a partial win
pairs.lesson: Both sides give something up, so it is partial or lose-lose. Trap: splitting a feature 50/50 is compromise, not collaboration.

pairs.right: The relationship matters more than the small point in dispute
pairs.lesson: Emphasizes agreement and downplays differences. It keeps harmony but is temporary, so the underlying issue may come back.

pairs.right: A safety, legal or ethics emergency needs an immediate decision
pairs.lesson: Win-lose and damaging if overused. Reserve it for urgent, non-negotiable situations where there is no time to collaborate.

pairs.right: Emotions run high and a short cool-down will help everyone
pairs.lesson: Generally the weakest choice. Acceptable only to let tempers cool or when the issue will resolve itself; never as a way to dodge a real problem.

sets.remember: Collaborate (time + both matter) > Compromise (deadline) > Smooth (relationship) > Force (emergency) > Withdraw (cool-down)

sets.title: Power types: spot them in action
sets.prompt: Match each type of power with the example that shows it in use.

pairs.right: PM assigns tasks citing authority granted in the project charter
pairs.lesson: Positional power from the role, granted by the charter or org structure. It disappears if the PM changes roles and is weak in functional or weak matrix organizations.

pairs.right: PM offers a bonus or public recognition for hitting the milestone
pairs.lesson: Positional power to give something people value. Works best when the reward is something the person actually values, which ties back to Vroom.

pairs.right: PM threatens a poor performance review if the deadline slips
pairs.lesson: Power through fear or punishment. Her notes call it the worst and a last resort; it damages trust and team performance.

pairs.right: Team follows the PM's advice because she has solved this problem before
pairs.lesson: Earned power from knowledge and skill. PMI favors it, with referent, because it works even without formal authority in a matrix. Her notes rank it best.

pairs.right: Team backs the PM because they respect and trust her personally
pairs.lesson: Earned power from relationships, respect and charisma. Strong emotional intelligence builds it over time; her notes rate it second best.

pairs.right: PM sways decisions because she controls key data and reports
pairs.lesson: Power from controlling access to information. Not one of French and Raven's original five; added later by Raven. Sharing information openly is the PMI-friendly stance.

sets.remember: Granted: Formal • Reward • Coercive  |  Earned: Expert • Referent  |  Plus: Informational (controls the data)

sets.title: Leadership styles: what you would see
sets.prompt: Match each leadership style with the behavior you would observe from a leader using it.

pairs.right: Removes impediments and shields the team so it can deliver
pairs.lesson: PMBOK 7's preferred style. Not passive: the leader actively unblocks, listens and empowers within boundaries. Total hands-off behavior is laissez-faire instead.

pairs.right: Adjusts direction and support to each person's skill and commitment
pairs.lesson: Hersey-Blanchard: directing, coaching, supporting, delegating. The same leader shifts style as the team or individual matures.

pairs.right: Inspires with a compelling vision and encourages fresh ideas
pairs.lesson: Leads through purpose and inspiration, pushing innovation and change. Spot it when the leader rallies people around a bigger why.

pairs.right: Sets clear targets and ties rewards or consequences to results
pairs.lesson: Management by exception and structured rewards; short-term focus. It can be right for clearly defined, routine work.

pairs.right: Steps back fully and lets a mature, expert team decide
pairs.lesson: Not automatically bad: right only for a mature, expert, self-sufficient team. Using it with a new team is a wrong answer.

pairs.right: Tells people exactly what to do and how during a crisis
pairs.lesson: Close, explicit direction. Fits a brand-new, inexperienced team or an emergency; overusing it with a capable team kills ownership.

sets.remember: Fit, not ranking: Servant (unblock) • Situational (adjust) • Transformational (inspire) • Transactional (reward) • Laissez-faire (step back) • Directive (tell)

sets.title: Emotional intelligence in everyday behavior
sets.prompt: Match each emotional intelligence component with the behavior that demonstrates it.

pairs.right: Notices her own rising frustration during a tense status meeting
pairs.lesson: Recognizing your own emotions as they happen. Trap: noticing is self-awareness; acting to calm down is self-regulation.

pairs.right: Pauses and calms down before replying to a harsh email
pairs.lesson: Also called self-management: controlling disruptive emotions and impulses. A PM who regulates first chooses a better conflict mode.

pairs.right: Stays driven by the goal itself despite repeated setbacks
pairs.lesson: In Goleman's five-component model, inner drive and optimism beyond money or status. The four-domain model folds this into self-management.

pairs.right: Senses a quiet member is worried and gently asks about it
pairs.lesson: Reading others' emotions; the four-domain model calls it social awareness. It powers active listening and spotting trouble early.

pairs.right: Builds rapport and guides two leads toward agreement
pairs.lesson: Relationship management: using the other components to influence, resolve conflict and build teams. It is how referent power grows.

sets.remember: Self (notice → regulate → motivate) then Others (empathy → social skill): recognize before you regulate

sets.title: Power/interest grid: engagement strategy
sets.prompt: Match each stakeholder position on the power/interest grid with the engagement strategy for it.

pairs.right: Manage closely: involve in key decisions and engage often
pairs.lesson: Key players such as the sponsor or a major customer. Full partnership, frequent two-way engagement and early involvement in decisions.

pairs.right: Keep satisfied: short summaries, no detail overload
pairs.lesson: Think a senior executive outside the project. Give enough attention to keep support; watch for interest rising, which moves them to manage closely.

pairs.right: Keep informed: regular updates and genuinely listen to input
pairs.lesson: End users or local community groups. Their input still matters and they can spot problems early; they can also influence those with power.

pairs.right: Monitor: minimal effort, check periodically for changes
pairs.lesson: Minimum effort is not zero effort. Every stakeholder gets baseline awareness, and positions can shift over time, so re-check the grid.

sets.remember: High/High = Manage closely • High/Low = Keep satisfied • Low/High = Keep informed • Low/Low = Monitor (know the ACTION, not just the box)

sets.title: Developing people: pick the right tool
sets.prompt: Match each people-development tool with the situation it fits best.

pairs.right: Several members lack a skill the new platform requires
pairs.lesson: Formal, structured learning for a skill gap, often for a group. Her rule: skill gap goes to training. Budget it in the resource plan.

pairs.right: A capable member's performance on one skill has slipped
pairs.lesson: Short-term, structured, goal-focused, one-to-one. A coach need not share the person's field. Address performance privately first, escalate only if unresolved.

pairs.right: A junior analyst wants guidance on their next five years
pairs.lesson: Long-term, informal and career-focused, usually with a senior person who walked a similar path. ECO tasks call out acting on mentoring opportunities.

pairs.right: A member just ran a workshop that needs specific improvements
pairs.lesson: Specific, timely comments on observed behavior, given privately when corrective. It is input for growth, not a formal development program.

pairs.right: A member's extra effort rescued last week's milestone
pairs.lesson: Most effective when specific, timely and matched to what the person values. Public recognition suits some people; others prefer a private thank-you.

sets.remember: Skill gap → Training • Performance → Coaching • Career → Mentoring • Moment → Feedback • Win → Recognition

sets.title: Remote teams: trust and safety practices
sets.prompt: Match each practice with the problem it solves on a virtual team.

pairs.right: Time zones leave no shared window for live collaboration
pairs.lesson: Agree a few hours when everyone is online for ceremonies and quick decisions. Her notes: establish working-hour overlap and time zone awareness.

pairs.right: Tone and intent keep getting lost in long email threads
pairs.lesson: Her order of richness: video beats audio, which beats email. Use richer channels for sensitive or complex conversations.

pairs.right: Remote members barely know each other as people
pairs.lesson: Trust grows from personal connection. Short social moments help build the belonging Maslow describes for isolated members.

pairs.right: Members clash over response times and meeting norms
pairs.lesson: A team charter or working agreement, created by the team and posted where everyone sees it, settles norms before they become conflicts.

pairs.right: Incident reviews keep turning into finger-pointing sessions
pairs.lesson: Focus on the process, not the person. Psychological safety lets problems surface early, which PMI strongly favors.

pairs.right: Team believes the PM expects flawless work from everyone
pairs.lesson: When the leader models candor, others feel safe to raise risks and errors. Servant leaders build safety by example, not by announcement.

sets.remember: Over-communicate • Overlap hours • Video > audio > email • Visible agreements • Blame the process, not the person

sets.title: Quality tools: the question each answers
sets.prompt: Match each quality tool with the question it helps the team answer.

pairs.right: How many times is each type of defect showing up?
pairs.lesson: A simple tally form used while inspecting. It collects the raw counts that later feed a Pareto chart or histogram. Think: gather the data first.

pairs.right: Where in our process steps could errors or delays creep in?
pairs.lesson: Maps the sequence of steps, decisions, and handoffs. Use it to spot rework loops and weak handoffs before defects happen. Prevention mindset.

pairs.right: Which few causes are producing most of our problems?
pairs.lesson: Bars sorted largest to smallest with a cumulative line, the 80/20 rule. It does not find causes; it ranks them so you fix the vital few first.

pairs.right: What are all the possible causes behind this one effect?
pairs.lesson: Also called Ishikawa or cause-and-effect. The team brainstorms causes by category. Trap: Fishbone lists causes, Pareto prioritizes them, 5 Whys drills deeper.

pairs.right: Is this process stable and running within its limits over time?
pairs.lesson: Shows data against upper and lower control limits. Seven points in a row on one side of the mean signals a problem even inside the limits.

pairs.right: Do two variables move together, and how strongly?
pairs.lesson: Plots one variable against another, such as training hours versus defects. A tight pattern suggests correlation, but correlation alone does not prove cause.

sets.remember: Count it (check sheet) → Map it (flowchart) → Brainstorm causes (fishbone) → Rank causes (Pareto) → Watch stability (control chart) → Test relationships (scatter)

sets.title: Estimating techniques: when to reach for each
sets.prompt: Match each estimating technique with the situation where it is the best choice.

pairs.right: Very early, little detail, and a similar past project exists
pairs.lesson: Top-down, fastest, least accurate. Uses actual results from a similar past project. Exam clue: charter stage, sponsor wants a quick rough number.

pairs.right: Reliable unit rate and quantity data are available
pairs.lesson: Rate times quantity, such as cost per square foot times square feet. Accuracy depends on how good the underlying rate is.

pairs.right: High uncertainty and you want best and worst cases weighed
pairs.lesson: Uses optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values. Beta formula is (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6. Good when risk makes a single-point estimate misleading.

pairs.right: Work is fully decomposed and the highest accuracy is required
pairs.lesson: Estimate each work package, then roll up. Slowest but most accurate. Needs a detailed WBS, so it is not possible very early.

pairs.right: Novel work where specialists' experience must fill data gaps
pairs.lesson: Draws on people who have done similar work. Often combined with other techniques. Trap: it is a supplement, not an excuse to skip analysis.

sets.remember: Analogous = similar past project • Parametric = rate × quantity • PERT = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 • Bottom-up = add up the pieces • Expert = specialists fill gaps

sets.title: Schedule fixes: spot the trigger words
sets.prompt: Match each schedule technique with the situation that calls for it.

pairs.right: Date must come earlier and extra budget is available
pairs.lesson: Add resources to critical-path activities to shorten them. Increases cost. Trap: crashing a non-critical activity does not shorten the project at all.

pairs.right: Date must come earlier, no extra money, rework risk acceptable
pairs.lesson: Run activities in parallel that were planned in sequence. No added cost, but more risk of rework. Works only where the logic is discretionary.

pairs.right: Shared specialist is overbooked and the end date may slip
pairs.lesson: Adjusts start and finish dates to fix resource conflicts. It can change the critical path and extend the schedule. Use when resources are the binding limit.

pairs.right: Workload is uneven but the finish date must not move
pairs.lesson: Evens out resource peaks only within available float. The critical path and end date stay the same. Memory: smoothing stays inside float.

pairs.right: Successor can safely start a few days before predecessor finishes
pairs.lesson: Overlaps linked activities, for example testing starts three days before coding ends. Shown as negative time on the dependency. Adds some rework risk.

pairs.right: A required waiting period must pass between linked activities
pairs.lesson: Inserts delay on a dependency, like concrete curing two days before framing. It is not float; the wait is built into the logic.

sets.remember: Money available → crash • No money → fast-track • Resource conflict → level (date can move) • Uneven load → smooth (date fixed)

sets.title: Dependencies and precedence logic
sets.prompt: Match each dependency type or precedence relationship with its defining rule.

pairs.right: Hard logic required by physics, law, or contract; cannot be reordered
pairs.lesson: You must pour the foundation before building walls. These links are never removed when fast-tracking because the sequence is unavoidable.

pairs.right: Soft logic based on best practice; team may change the order
pairs.lesson: Preferred sequence from experience. These are the links you can relax when fast-tracking. Document why they exist so nobody removes them blindly.

pairs.right: Relies on parties outside the project, like regulators or vendors
pairs.lesson: The project team does not control it, such as a permit approval. Track these closely as risks because the PM cannot simply speed them up.

pairs.right: The next activity waits until the previous one is complete
pairs.lesson: The most common relationship and the default in most network diagrams. Example: approve design, then begin construction.

pairs.right: The next activity may begin once the previous one has begun
pairs.lesson: Both can run in parallel after the first starts, often with a lag. Example: editing starts two days after writing starts.

pairs.right: The next activity cannot be complete until the previous one is
pairs.lesson: Endings are linked, not beginnings. Example: testing cannot finish until development finishes. Start-to-finish is the rare trap answer.

sets.remember: Mandatory = must • Discretionary = prefer • External = outside control • FS is the default; SF is the rare trap

sets.title: EVM measures: the question behind each
sets.prompt: Match each earned value measure with the question it answers for the project manager.

pairs.right: How much work, in dollars, did we plan to finish by now?
pairs.lesson: The authorized budget for work scheduled to date. PV tells where I planned to be. Its total at the end equals BAC.

pairs.right: How much budgeted work, in dollars, have we truly completed?
pairs.lesson: Value of work actually done, measured in budget terms. EV tells where I really am. Every EVM formula starts from EV.

pairs.right: What have we really spent to complete the work so far?
pairs.lesson: Actual money spent for the work performed. AC tells what the journey has cost. Never compare AC with PV directly; compare with EV.

pairs.right: How many dollars of work are we ahead of or behind?
pairs.lesson: SV = EV − PV. Negative means behind schedule. It is measured in money, which surprises students, and returns to zero at project end.

pairs.right: How much value are we earning for each dollar spent?
pairs.lesson: CPI = EV ÷ AC. Below 1.0 means over budget. A CPI of 0.80 means only 80 cents of value for every dollar spent.

pairs.right: At what rate are we progressing compared with the plan?
pairs.lesson: SPI = EV ÷ PV. Below 1.0 means behind schedule. Use with the critical path, because SPI alone can hide late critical work.

sets.remember: Plan it (PV) → Earn it (EV) → Spend it (AC) → Compare it (CV, SV, CPI, SPI) → Forecast it (EAC)

sets.title: EVM forecasts: which formula when
sets.prompt: Match each forecasting formula with the situation in which you would use it.

pairs.right: Current cost efficiency is expected to continue for the remaining work
pairs.lesson: The typical-variance formula. If today's overspending pattern will persist, scale the whole budget by CPI. Most common exam default when nothing else is said.

pairs.right: Past variance was a one-time event; remaining work goes to plan
