pairs.lesson: The atypical formula. Spent money stays spent, and the rest of the work costs what was originally budgeted. Clue words: unusual, one-time, will not recur.

pairs.right: Both cost and schedule pressure will shape the rest of the spending
pairs.lesson: Used when a hard deadline means poor schedule performance will also drive cost, for example overtime to recover. Usually the most pessimistic forecast when both indices are below 1.0.

pairs.right: Original estimates are no longer valid, so remaining work is re-estimated
pairs.lesson: When assumptions were flawed, re-estimate what is left from the bottom up and add it to what has been spent. ETC itself means money still needed.

pairs.right: Sponsor wants to know the expected budget gap at the finish
pairs.lesson: Positive is good, negative means finishing over budget. If BAC is $1M and EAC is $1.2M, VAC is −$200K.

pairs.right: Asks what efficiency the remaining work needs to hit a target
pairs.lesson: (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) to hit BAC. Above 1.0 means you must work harder than before. Use EAC in the denominator once BAC is unrealistic.

sets.remember: BAC = original • EAC = forecast • ETC = what's left • VAC = final gap • TCPI = effort needed

sets.title: Cost of quality: where the money goes
sets.prompt: Match each cost of quality category with an example of spending in it.

pairs.right: Training the team and writing standards before any work begins
pairs.lesson: Cost of conformance spent to stop defects from being created. PMI prefers prevention over inspection; more prevention usually lowers total failure cost.

pairs.right: Testing, inspections, and audits to measure whether work conforms
pairs.lesson: Also cost of conformance, spent to find defects. Inspection still matters to confirm results, but it is not the first quality mindset.

pairs.right: Rework and scrap caught by the team before the customer sees it
pairs.lesson: Cost of nonconformance found inside the project. Painful but cheaper than letting the defect escape to the customer.

pairs.right: Warranty claims, recalls, and lost reputation after delivery
pairs.lesson: Cost of nonconformance found by the customer. Usually the most damaging because it hits trust, safety, and compliance, not just money.

sets.remember: Conformance = Prevention + Appraisal • Nonconformance = Internal + External failure • Prevent before you inspect

sets.title: Group techniques: read the clue
sets.prompt: Match each data-gathering or decision technique with the clue that points to it on the exam.

pairs.right: Need lots of ideas quickly, quantity first, no judging yet
pairs.lesson: Free-flowing idea generation in a group. Volume over structure. Often followed by an affinity diagram or nominal group voting to organize the ideas.

pairs.right: Ideas generated silently, shared round-robin, then ranked by vote
pairs.lesson: Brainstorming plus structured silent ranking. The voting step is the clue. Gives quieter members an equal voice.

pairs.right: Experts must stay anonymous so strong voices cannot sway others
pairs.lesson: Anonymous questionnaires go out in multiple rounds through a facilitator until opinions converge. Trap: a focus group is face-to-face; Delphi is anonymous.

pairs.right: Options are scored against weighted criteria in a matrix
pairs.lesson: Use when choosing between vendors, designs, or approaches using several factors such as cost, risk, and quality, each with a weight.

pairs.right: Choosing between paths using probabilities and payoffs at each branch
pairs.lesson: Calculates expected monetary value for each branch, then picks the best. Clue: a build-versus-buy choice with percentages and dollar outcomes.

pairs.right: Thousands of computer runs show odds of hitting the overall date
pairs.lesson: A quantitative risk tool that models the whole project using ranges. Output is a probability curve, such as 80 percent confidence of finishing by June.

sets.remember: Ideas → Brainstorm • Rank → Nominal group • Anonymous → Delphi • Weighted options → Multicriteria • Branches + EMV → Decision tree • Whole-project odds → Monte Carlo

sets.title: Communication methods: know the weak spot
sets.prompt: Match each communication method with its main weakness the project manager must manage.

pairs.right: Hard to schedule across many people and time zones; capture decisions afterward
pairs.lesson: Meetings, calls, video conferences. Best for complex or sensitive topics because understanding is confirmed in real time. Record decisions in minutes.

pairs.right: Sent does not mean read or understood; confirm critical messages
pairs.lesson: Emails, memos, reports sent to specific people. Exam trap: if confirmed understanding was required, push alone was the wrong choice.

pairs.right: Recipients may never look, so it suits large audiences, not urgent news
pairs.lesson: Intranets, wikis, knowledge bases that people visit at their own pace. Great for reference material and large groups, poor for must-know-now messages.

pairs.right: Remote members miss what colocated teammates overhear
pairs.lesson: Information absorbed by sitting together in an agile team room. Distributed teams must replace it with open video channels and team chat.

sets.remember: Must confirm it → Interactive • Must send it → Push • Many need it sometime → Pull • Overhear it → Osmotic

sets.title: Threat responses: what changes afterward
sets.prompt: Match each threat response with what it changes about the risk.

pairs.right: Probability drops to zero because the plan is changed to remove it
pairs.lesson: Eliminate the threat by changing scope, schedule, or approach, like dropping an unproven technology. Only response that removes the threat completely.

pairs.right: Financial impact shifts to a third party; the risk still exists
pairs.lesson: Insurance, warranties, fixed-price contracts. The buyer pays a premium, and the threat itself does not disappear. Memory: insurance = transfer.

pairs.right: Chance or impact is lowered, but some exposure stays with the project
pairs.lesson: Extra testing, prototypes, redundant suppliers. Proactive action taken now. Trap: a fallback plan used after it occurs is contingency, not mitigation.

pairs.right: Nothing is reduced; the team acknowledges it and watches it
pairs.lesson: Passive acceptance does nothing; active acceptance sets aside contingency reserve. Used when no cost-effective response exists or the threat is small.

pairs.right: Ownership moves above the project manager to a higher authority
pairs.lesson: Use when the threat is outside project scope or beyond the PM's authority. Once accepted by the program or portfolio owner, it is no longer tracked by the project.

sets.remember: Threats = A-M-T-A + Escalate • Avoid = eliminate • Mitigate = reduce • Transfer = shift • Accept = acknowledge

sets.title: Opportunity responses: example actions
sets.prompt: Match each opportunity response with an action that shows it.

pairs.right: Assign the top engineer so the early-finish bonus is guaranteed
pairs.lesson: Make the opportunity certain, raising probability to 100 percent. The opportunity version of avoid. Clue words: ensure, guarantee, lock in.

pairs.right: Form a joint venture with a partner to capture a new market
pairs.lesson: Give part ownership to a third party better able to seize it. The opportunity version of transfer. Both sides gain from the upside.

pairs.right: Add training to raise the chance the team finishes early
pairs.lesson: Increase probability or impact without making it certain. The opportunity version of mitigate. Clue words: increase, improve the odds.

pairs.right: Welcome the windfall if it arrives, but take no special action
pairs.lesson: Acknowledge the opportunity and do nothing proactive. Fine for small upsides or when pursuing them costs more than they return.

pairs.right: Pass it to the portfolio owner because it sits beyond the project
pairs.lesson: The opportunity is real but outside project scope or PM authority. Hand it to the right level so the organization can still benefit.

sets.remember: Opportunities = E-E-S-A + Escalate • Exploit = make it happen • Enhance = increase • Share = partner • Accept = acknowledge

sets.title: Risk, issue, assumption, or constraint?
sets.prompt: Match each term with the statement that shows it.

pairs.right: The vendor might deliver the servers two weeks late
pairs.lesson: Uncertain future event that could help or hurt. Clue words: may, might, could, potential. Lives in the risk register with an owner.

pairs.right: The vendor's servers did not arrive on the agreed date
pairs.lesson: It has already happened and needs action now. Lives in the issue log. Risk is the storm forecast; issue is standing in the rain.

pairs.right: We believe the vendor will deliver on time, though unproven
pairs.lesson: Treated as true for planning without proof. Record it in the assumption log and validate it, because a false assumption becomes a risk.

pairs.right: Contract requires all servers installed before the fiscal year ends
pairs.lesson: A fixed limit the project must work within, such as a date, budget, or regulation. Not uncertain, so it is not a risk.

pairs.right: The factory warns the vendor of a parts shortage this week
pairs.lesson: An early warning sign that a risk is about to occur. The risk owner watches for it and launches the planned response.

sets.remember: Assumption (believed) → Risk (may happen) → Trigger (warning sign) → Issue (has happened) • Constraint = fixed limit

sets.title: Reserves and risk tolerance terms
sets.prompt: Match each risk term with its meaning.

pairs.right: Exposure left over after the planned response is carried out
pairs.lesson: Expected to remain even when the response works. Record it and accept it, often with contingency. Not a new risk, just what is left.

pairs.right: New exposure created by carrying out a response
pairs.lesson: Example: hiring a second vendor to mitigate delay introduces coordination risk. Analyze it like any other risk and log it.

pairs.right: Money or time for identified risks, controlled by the PM
pairs.lesson: Covers known unknowns and is inside the cost baseline. The PM can use it per the risk management plan without a change request.

pairs.right: Funds for unforeseen work, held outside the baseline by management
pairs.lesson: Covers unknown unknowns. Using it requires management approval and a change request because it adds to the cost baseline.

pairs.right: How much uncertainty the organization will accept in pursuit of reward
pairs.lesson: A broad, qualitative attitude set by leaders. A startup may have high appetite; a hospital usually low. It shapes risk thresholds.

pairs.right: Measurable exposure level above which a risk needs action or escalation
pairs.lesson: Turns appetite into numbers, such as any risk over $50K goes to the sponsor. Defined in the risk management plan.

sets.remember: Residual = left over • Secondary = newly created • Contingency = known unknowns (PM) • Management reserve = unknown unknowns (management)

sets.title: Risk analysis tools: what each produces
sets.prompt: Match each risk analysis tool with what it produces.

pairs.right: Places each risk in high, medium, or low priority zones
pairs.lesson: Qualitative tool. Answers which risks matter most. Fast and subjective, done for nearly every project before any numeric modeling.

pairs.right: A judgment of how reliable and complete each risk's information is
pairs.lesson: Qualitative. If the data is weak, the ranking is weak. Clue: team doubts the accuracy of the risk information before prioritizing.

pairs.right: Flags risks needing action soon because their window is short
pairs.lesson: Qualitative. A risk can be medium score but urgent if its trigger is close. Urgency is one of the extra dimensions alongside probability and impact.

pairs.right: A probability-weighted dollar figure, such as 30% × $100K
pairs.lesson: Quantitative. Positive for opportunities, negative for threats. It is an average expected value, not a guarantee.

pairs.right: Odds of meeting the overall date or budget from thousands of runs
pairs.lesson: Quantitative and done on the whole project, not single risks. Output is an S-curve showing confidence levels.

pairs.right: Bars ranking which risks swing the project result the most
pairs.lesson: Quantitative sensitivity analysis. The widest bar on top has the biggest influence on the outcome. Focus responses there first.

sets.remember: Qualitative asks 'Which risks matter most?' → Quantitative asks 'How much could they affect us?' (quantitative is not always required)

sets.title: Contract types: when each fits
sets.prompt: Match each contract type with the situation where it fits best.

pairs.right: Scope is clear and stable; buyer wants total price certainty
pairs.lesson: Seller carries the most cost risk. Trap: vague scope under fixed price still creates disputes and change requests.

pairs.right: Defined scope, plus a bonus for hitting measurable targets
pairs.lesson: Price is capped with a ceiling, and the seller earns extra for beating cost or performance goals. Risk shared but leaning to the seller.

pairs.right: Multi-year deal exposed to inflation or commodity price swings
pairs.lesson: Price adjusts by an agreed index such as a cost of steel index. Protects both sides over long periods.

pairs.right: Uncertain scope, and seller's profit is agreed upfront and never varies
pairs.lesson: Buyer reimburses allowable costs plus a set fee. Buyer carries the cost risk; seller has little incentive to save.

pairs.right: Complex work where the buyer judges performance subjectively
pairs.lesson: Buyer reimburses costs, and the award fee is decided by the buyer's assessment. The decision usually cannot be appealed.

pairs.right: Short, urgent staff help needed before scope can be defined
pairs.lesson: Hourly rates plus materials. Buyer carries risk unless capped. Set a not-to-exceed limit and track hours tightly.

sets.remember: Fixed price = seller carries cost risk • Cost reimbursable = buyer carries cost risk • T&M = watch scope and hours

sets.title: Seller selection: buyer's toolkit
sets.prompt: Match each seller selection term with its purpose.

pairs.right: Pass-fail filter that drops vendors missing a minimum requirement
pairs.lesson: Applied before detailed scoring, for example a required license or security clearance. Sellers who fail are dropped, so scoring effort goes only to viable proposals.

pairs.right: Meeting where all prospective sellers hear identical answers
pairs.lesson: Ensures fairness: no seller gets inside information. Answers are shared in writing with everyone. Trap: never answer one seller privately.

pairs.right: Approved yardsticks used to score and rank seller proposals
pairs.lesson: Includes capability, technical approach, risk, price, and past performance. Lowest price is not always best value.

pairs.right: Buyer's own figure used to sanity-check the sellers' prices
pairs.lesson: Prepared internally or by an outside estimator. A big gap with proposals suggests the SOW was unclear or sellers misunderstood.

pairs.right: Pre-screened vendors already vetted for capability
pairs.lesson: Kept in organizational process assets. Speeds solicitation, but still requires fair, documented evaluation.

pairs.right: Settles final terms and price with the preferred seller before signing
pairs.lesson: Happens after evaluation and before award. The aim is a fair, clear agreement both sides understand, not squeezing the seller; agreed terms then go into the contract.

sets.remember: Screen (pass/fail) → Score (criteria) → Sanity-check (independent estimate) → Negotiate → Award • Bidder conference keeps it fair

sets.title: Claims and disputes: the escalation ladder
sets.prompt: Match each step of handling a contract claim with what happens in it.

pairs.right: Contested change is formally raised with facts and supporting evidence
pairs.lesson: Follow the notice clause in the contract. Document impact on cost, time, or scope. Undocumented complaints carry little weight.

pairs.right: Buyer and seller try to settle the disagreement directly in good faith
pairs.lesson: PMI's preferred first resolution. Review the contract, discuss, and document every communication. Most claims end here.

pairs.right: Moves to higher management levels named in the agreement
pairs.lesson: Follow the escalation path written in the contract, not personal relationships. Still before any outside party is involved.

pairs.right: Neutral third party helps both sides reach a voluntary agreement
pairs.lesson: A form of alternative dispute resolution (ADR). The mediator suggests but cannot impose a decision.

pairs.right: Neutral party hears both sides and issues a usually binding decision
pairs.lesson: Also ADR, but more formal than mediation. Faster and private compared with court. Check whether the contract makes it binding.

pairs.right: Court case; the last resort after other paths fail
pairs.lesson: Costly, slow, and damaging to relationships. PMP trap: never jump to suing or terminating first unless severity or contract requires it.

sets.remember: Notify → Negotiate → Escalate → ADR (mediation, arbitration) → Litigation • Contract first, document everything, negotiate before escalating

sets.title: Clean procurement closure flow
sets.prompt: Match each step of closing a procurement with what happens in it.

pairs.right: Delivered work is checked against the SOW and acceptance criteria
pairs.lesson: Inspection before acceptance. Do not rely on the seller's word that all is done; compare against the contract terms.

pairs.right: Buyer formally signs off on the deliverables in writing
pairs.lesson: Formal written acceptance from the authorized person. Without it the contract is not complete, regardless of what was shipped.

pairs.right: Defects, punch-list items, and open claims are settled or transferred
pairs.lesson: Never close with unresolved obligations. Open claims are settled or formally transferred before the contract is closed.

pairs.right: Final invoice is reviewed and the last payment is released
pairs.lesson: Payment follows acceptance and invoice review, not before. Paying first removes the buyer's leverage.

pairs.right: Contracts, amendments, claims, and invoices are filed for the record
pairs.lesson: Procurement records may be needed for audits or future disputes. Part of organizational process assets.

pairs.right: Seller performance and procurement insights are captured for reuse
pairs.lesson: Feeds the lessons learned register and future qualified seller lists. Procurement closure can happen before project closure.

sets.remember: Verify → Accept → Resolve → Pay → Archive → Lessons • Do not just file it away

sets.title: Governance: who decides what
sets.prompt: Match each governance role or body with the decision it typically owns.

pairs.right: Provides funding and owns the business case for this project
pairs.lesson: The executive champion. Approves the charter and handles escalations beyond PM authority. If the business case weakens, consult the sponsor.

pairs.right: Senior cross-department group giving direction at gates and trade-offs
pairs.lesson: Brings together leaders from affected areas for major direction decisions and phase-gate reviews. Not involved in day-to-day work.

pairs.right: Approves or rejects requested changes to the project baselines
pairs.lesson: Formally chartered group named in the change management plan. The PM analyzes impact first; the CCB decides.

pairs.right: Sets project standards, templates, and reporting across the organization
pairs.lesson: Can be supportive, controlling, or directive. Provides governance, training, and oversight, but usually does not approve individual changes.

pairs.right: Selects, prioritizes, and funds projects based on strategic fit
pairs.lesson: Decides which projects start, continue, or stop. Portfolio = strategy. A project losing alignment may be cancelled here.

pairs.right: Makes day-to-day decisions within delegated authority and tolerances
pairs.lesson: Manages within the authority granted by the charter. Assess and act within limits; escalate only when outside that authority.

sets.remember: Governance = Authority • Ask: sponsor, steering committee, CCB, PMO, portfolio board, or PM? Check authority, then act within it

sets.title: External change and compliance: first moves
sets.prompt: Match each business environment situation with the project manager's best first response.

pairs.right: Assess impact with legal or compliance experts, then use change control
pairs.lesson: Compliance is mandatory, but do not change the project instantly. Assess, consult the subject matter expert, route through change control, then update plans.

pairs.left: Team wants to skip safety documentation
pairs.right: Refuse; complete the required records even if the schedule suffers
pairs.lesson: Mandatory beats optional. Compliance cannot be traded for cost or schedule. You follow the rule, then capture the lesson.

pairs.right: Correct the records, document the fix, and remove the root cause
pairs.lesson: Compliance flow: assess, correct, document, prevent recurrence. Blaming the team or hiding the gap are both wrong answers.

pairs.right: Review the business case and benefits with the sponsor before continuing
pairs.lesson: The market shift may change value. Do not continue just because the charter was approved; reassess alignment with the sponsor and governance.

pairs.right: Analyze cost impact, check contract terms, and inform the sponsor
pairs.lesson: Economic change hits the budget. Look at the contract, such as an economic price adjustment clause, assess reserves, then raise a change request if needed.

pairs.right: Work out how the goals apply and add them to planning criteria
pairs.lesson: Not explicitly in scope does not mean the project can ignore organizational strategy. Assess and incorporate relevant criteria through proper channels.

sets.remember: Calculate/Assess → Interpret → Check governance/compliance → Decide → Monitor • Compliance: Assess → Consult SME → Correct → Document → Prevent recurrence

sets.title: Value chain: one CRM project traced
sets.prompt: For a company rolling out a new CRM system, match each value term with its example.

pairs.right: Configured system installed, tested, and handed to the sales team
pairs.lesson: The tangible deliverable the project produces. Accepting an output does not guarantee anyone uses it or that value follows.

pairs.right: Sales reps now log every customer call in the new tool
pairs.lesson: The change in behavior or capability that the output enables. Adoption is the bridge from output to outcome.

pairs.right: Customer retention rises eight percent within the first year
pairs.lesson: Measurable gain from the outcome, often realized after project closure. Tracked against targets in the benefits management plan.

pairs.right: Organization is stronger overall: more revenue, loyalty, and strategic edge
pairs.lesson: The overall worth to stakeholders, weighing benefits against cost and risk. Value is the reason the project exists.

pairs.right: Sales vice president who tracks retention gains after handover
pairs.lesson: Usually a business or operational leader, not the PM. Keeps measuring benefits long after the project team has disbanded.

pairs.right: Defines targets, timing, metrics, and who measures each gain
pairs.lesson: Created early alongside the business case and used to judge whether expected value actually happened.

sets.remember: Output (we built it) → Outcome (they use it) → Benefit (it pays off) → Value (it was worth it)

sets.title: Financial measures: the decision rule
sets.prompt: Match each financial measure with the rule a selection committee applies to it.

pairs.right: Positive dollar figure today means the project creates value
pairs.lesson: Discounts future cash flows to today's dollars. Higher positive NPV preferred. NPV already accounts for project life, so do not adjust for years again.

pairs.right: Pick the higher percentage, as long as it beats the hurdle rate
pairs.lesson: The discount rate at which NPV equals zero. IRR is a percentage; NPV is money. When they conflict, NPV usually wins.

pairs.right: Above 1.0 means benefits outweigh costs; higher is better
pairs.lesson: Benefits divided by costs. A BCR of 1.5 returns $1.50 per dollar spent. Do not confuse with ROI, which uses net benefit.

pairs.right: Shorter is better, but cash after break-even is ignored
pairs.lesson: Measures speed of recovering the investment, not total lifetime value. Useful when cash or risk is tight.

pairs.right: Value of the best alternative given up by choosing this one
pairs.lesson: If you pick project A worth $500K over project B worth $400K, the opportunity cost is $400K.

pairs.right: Ignore it; money already spent should not drive future choices
pairs.lesson: Gone money. The trap is continuing a failing project because so much has been spent. Evaluate future value instead.

sets.remember: ROI = Return • NPV = Value • IRR = Rate • Payback = Time • Opportunity cost = Lost alternative • Sunk cost = Gone money

sets.title: Change models: what each focuses on
sets.prompt: Match each organizational change model with what it focuses on.

pairs.right: One person at a time builds understanding, willingness, skill, and lasting habit
pairs.lesson: Prosci's model focuses on one person at a time. Find the first blocked step: training will not help someone who lacks desire.

pairs.right: Leaders build urgency and a coalition, then anchor change in culture
pairs.lesson: Organization-wide, top-down sequence: urgency, coalition, vision, communicate, remove obstacles, quick wins, build on change, anchor it.

pairs.right: Performance dips into chaos after a foreign element, then recovers higher
pairs.lesson: Late status quo, foreign element, chaos, transforming idea, practice and integration, new status quo. Expect the productivity dip; it is normal, not a sign of failure.

pairs.right: People pass through an ending, a neutral zone, then a new beginning
pairs.lesson: Separates the external change from the internal psychological transition. Leaders must help people let go before they can embrace the new.

pairs.right: Unfreeze the current state, make the change, refreeze it as the norm
pairs.lesson: Simple and classic. The refreeze stage is why reinforcement matters; without it people slide back to old habits.

sets.remember: ADKAR = the individual • Kotter = the organization's leaders • Satir = the performance curve • Bridges = the emotional transition • Lewin = unfreeze → change → refreeze

sets.title: Org structures: who controls the team
sets.prompt: Match each organizational structure with who controls the project's resources and budget.

pairs.right: Work stays inside one department, whose head controls people and budget
pairs.lesson: Team members report to their department head and project work is done within that department. The PM role, if any, is part-time with little or no authority.

pairs.right: Cross-department team; functional managers keep the budget, PM mostly coordinates
pairs.lesson: PM has low authority, often acting part-time as an expediter or coordinator. Resource conflicts go to the functional manager first.

pairs.right: PM and department managers share control of budget and people
pairs.lesson: Power shared, so negotiation is constant. Two-boss situations are common; agree on priorities early.

pairs.right: Full-time PM controls most of the budget; staff still have home departments
pairs.lesson: PM authority is moderate to high and often sits in a PMO. Team members return to their departments after the project.

pairs.right: PM controls budget and a dedicated full-time team with no home department
pairs.lesson: PM has high to almost total authority. Team may have nowhere to go when the project ends, so plan release carefully.

sets.remember: Functional → Weak → Balanced → Strong → Projectized • PM power grows left to right; functional manager power shrinks

sets.title: Life cycles: choose by the clue
sets.prompt: Match each development life cycle with the situation that best calls for it.

pairs.right: Requirements are stable and well known, and change is costly
pairs.lesson: Plan upfront, control to the baseline. Example: building a bridge to a fixed regulatory design. Know it and control it.

pairs.right: Solution is unclear, so the same prototype is refined through repeated cycles
pairs.lesson: Improve the same thing until it is right. Iterative remodels the same kitchen. Focus is learning and refinement, not early delivery.

pairs.right: Customer wants usable pieces early, each adding to what already works
pairs.lesson: Add usable parts in sequence. Incremental adds one room at a time. Clue: new working features delivered regularly.

pairs.right: Needs keep changing, and frequent customer feedback steers each cycle
pairs.lesson: Agile approaches combine iterative and incremental with ongoing feedback. Learn and adapt. Clue: high uncertainty and evolving requirements.

pairs.right: Some parts are fixed and regulated while others are uncertain and evolving
pairs.lesson: Intentionally blend approaches by need, such as predictive hardware with adaptive software. Not a default 50/50 compromise; it must be justified.

sets.remember: Stable = Predictive • Refine = Iterative • Add parts = Incremental • Changing = Adaptive • Mixed = Hybrid

sets.title: EEF or OPA: sort the example
sets.prompt: Match each example with the explanation of whether it is an EEF or an OPA and why.

pairs.right: EEF: an outside legal rule the project must obey
pairs.lesson: Enterprise environmental factors are conditions not under the team's control. Fast test: government regulation? EEF.

pairs.right: OPA: a reusable form from the organization's process library
pairs.lesson: Organizational process assets are the company's own plans, processes, and knowledge. Fast test: company template? OPA.

pairs.right: EEF: internal climate and values shaping how work gets done
pairs.lesson: EEFs can be internal too. Culture, structure, and governance style are internal EEFs, not process assets.

pairs.right: OPA: stored knowledge from past projects ready for reuse
pairs.lesson: Historical information and lessons learned are part of the corporate knowledge base. Check it during planning, update it during closure.

pairs.right: EEF: external economic situation affecting cost, demand, and suppliers
pairs.lesson: External EEF. Competition, pricing, and supplier availability influence the project, but the PM cannot change them.

pairs.right: OPA: a defined company process for handling requested modifications
pairs.lesson: Policies and procedures are OPAs. The project follows and may tailor them, and can suggest improvements for future projects.

sets.remember: EEF = the environment you operate within • OPA = the organization's own knowledge and processes • Regulation → EEF • Template → OPA

sets.title: Responsible AI and sustainability: PM actions
sets.prompt: Match each AI or sustainability concern with what the project manager should do about it.

pairs.right: Validate AI-generated facts against trusted sources before anyone uses them
pairs.lesson: Hallucinations sound plausible but are wrong. AI can draft and recommend; humans check and stay accountable for what goes out.

pairs.right: Review outputs for unfair patterns and test with diverse data
pairs.lesson: Bias is systematic unfairness in data or decisions. Ignoring it because output is fast is a classic wrong answer.

pairs.right: Monitor accuracy over time and retrain when real data shifts
pairs.lesson: A model that worked at launch can degrade as conditions change. Assign ownership for ongoing monitoring after handover.

pairs.right: Use only approved tools and remove sensitive information first
pairs.lesson: Protect data first. Pasting client or personal data into an unapproved public tool breaks privacy and security policies.

pairs.right: Back every environmental claim with measured, verifiable evidence
pairs.lesson: Overstating green credentials damages trust and can breach regulations. ESG reporting needs real data, not marketing language.

pairs.right: Compare total long-term cost, waste, and energy, not just purchase price
pairs.lesson: Sustainability is environmental, social, and economic. A cheaper option that wastes energy and breaks often may fail every dimension.

sets.remember: AI: Protect data → Validate output → Human decides • Sustainability: Evaluate lifecycle impact → Balance value, cost, risk → Think long term
